strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel construction—vector diffusion wavelets built from vector diffusion maps (Singer & Wu)—that extends scattering transforms to geometric graphs with vector-valued features, addressing a real gap since prior scattering-transform papers only handled scalar signals.

Provides rigorous theoretical support: frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) showing stability/invertibility of the new wavelet transform, and equivariance proofs (Theorems 3.2 and 3.3) for the wavelets and resulting scattering coefficients, with detailed, mostly self-contained proofs in the appendix.
Careful handling of the SVD sign ambiguity issue that arises when building local coordinate frames, with an explicit, well-justified fix (Appendix C).

Demonstrates substantial parameter efficiency: comparable or only slightly worse accuracy than EGNN/TFN while using a small fraction (often <1%) of the parameters, which is a practically meaningful contribution given the extensive appendix discussion of computational complexity and runtimes.
The ablation comparing equivariant vs. non-equivariant versions of the same architecture cleanly demonstrates the practical value of the proposed equivariant design on the rotated test set.
Well-organized background sections situate the work clearly relative to message-passing GNNs, scattering transforms, and existing equivariant GNN frameworks.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted exclusively on synthetic ellipsoid point-cloud data with only two tasks (diameter regression and normal-vector prediction); despite motivating the method with molecular graphs and real-world applications (binding affinity, polar surface area) in the introduction, no real-world or standard benchmark (e.g., QM9, MD17, N-body simulation) is used to validate the approach, limiting confidence in the method's practical significance.

The abstract and title claim SE(3)-equivariance, but the formal theorems (3.2, 3.3) only establish SO(d) (rotation) equivariance; translation invariance is only implicit via the use of relative coordinates in constructing Q and is never explicitly stated or proven as a theorem, leaving a gap between the claimed and proven symmetry group.

Test-set rotation is limited to a single, fixed 90-degree rotation rather than a broader sweep over SO(3), making it a fairly weak empirical test of equivariance robustness compared to what is typically done in the equivariant GNN literature.

On the node-level task, TFN outperforms the proposed ESc-GNN (Table 2), and the parameter-efficiency argument, while notable, does not fully offset the fact that the method is not shown to be superior in accuracy to strong existing equivariant baselines on either task.

Reported standard deviations across 5-fold CV are often very large relative to the means (e.g., non-equivariant baselines, LEGS), raising questions about the statistical robustness of the comparisons given the small, synthetic dataset (512 graphs).

The local SVD-based frame construction assumes non-degenerate, non-repeated singular values and sufficient neighbor counts (ni ≥ d); the paper does not discuss or empirically test robustness when neighborhoods are close to isotropic or degenerate, which could be common in real point clouds/molecules and could destabilize the sign-disambiguation procedure.

Only a single vector-valued feature channel (3D coordinates) is used in experiments, so the framework's stated ability to jointly process multiple scalar and vector signals is not empirically demonstrated.
No code repository link is provided in the submitted text (placeholder left blank), which limits verifiability of reproducibility claims, though this may be an anonymization artifact.

The motivating claim about avoiding the oversmoothing/underreaching tradeoff via multiscale wavelets is not directly tested via an experiment isolating long-range dependency benefits (e.g., varying graph diameter or depth requirements), despite being a central motivation in the introduction.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel theoretical construction—vector diffusion wavelets built from vector diffusion maps (Singer & Wu)—extending geometric scattering transforms to vector-valued node features, which is a meaningful conceptual contribution to the scattering-transform literature.

The theoretical development is rigorous: frame bounds (Thm 3.1), wavelet equivariance (Thm 3.2), and scattering coefficient equivariance (Thm 3.3) are proved in detail, with careful treatment of the SVD sign ambiguity (Appendix C) that is often glossed over in related constructions.

The paper clearly demonstrates a strong parameter-efficiency advantage: the proposed ESc-GNN achieves performance comparable to EGNN and TFN while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters (e.g., 57K vs 29.6M for TFN), which is a practically relevant finding for lightweight equivariant modeling.
Good supporting visualizations (Figures 1 and 2) intuitively illustrate the rotational equivariance of the vector diffusion operator and wavelets.
Reasonably thorough appendix with complexity analysis, runtime tables, and detailed architecture/hyperparameter descriptions, aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on small, synthetic ellipsoid point-cloud datasets (512 graphs, 128 points) rather than standard real-world equivariant-GNN benchmarks (e.g., QM9, MD17, N-body simulation), which severely limits the ability to judge practical significance and generalizability of the method.

Results show large variance (e.g., std comparable to or exceeding the mean in several MSE entries in Tables 1-2), raising doubts about the statistical reliability of the comparisons given only 5-fold CV on such small datasets.

On the node-level task, TFN actually outperforms the proposed method, undermining the paper's central claim of 'comparable performance with far fewer parameters'; the paper frames this inconsistently as still supporting its thesis.

The reported TFN parameter counts (29M+) seem unusually large relative to typical TFN configurations in the literature, suggesting the baseline may not be optimally configured, which makes the 'fraction of the parameters' comparison less convincing as a fair baseline comparison.

No ablations isolating the contribution of design choices such as second-order scattering coefficients, number of wavelet scales, the InfoGain scale-selection procedure vs. dyadic scales, or the vector-invariant extraction layer, making it hard to assess which components drive performance.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section in the main text discussing the restriction to synthetic data, the dmin/dmax dependency of the frame bound (which could be very loose for graphs with heterogeneous degree), or the lack of translation equivariance discussion despite claiming SE(3)-equivariance in the abstract (only SO(d) is proven).
The code repository link in the reproducibility appendix (E) appears incomplete/blank, undermining full reproducibility claims.
No comparison, empirical or otherwise, against closely related manifold/vector scattering approaches (e.g., Chew et al. manifold scattering) that are discussed in related work but not benchmarked.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution—extending diffusion wavelets and geometric scattering to vector-valued signals via a vector diffusion matrix Q built from local SVD-based coordinate frames (inspired by Singer & Wu's vector diffusion maps)—is novel and well-motivated, addressing a genuine gap since prior geometric scattering work (Chew et al., Johnson et al.) did not handle vector-valued node features.

The theoretical development is careful and complete: frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) establishing stability/invertibility, and rigorous equivariance proofs (Theorems 3.2, 3.3) with full derivations in the appendix, including a sign-ambiguity resolution for the SVD-based local frames (Appendix C) that is a practically important but easy-to-overlook detail.

The paper clearly motivates the approach by connecting to the well-known oversmoothing/underreaching tradeoff in message-passing GNNs, situating the contribution within established literature on scattering transforms.

Empirical results show the method is competitive with much more heavyweight equivariant baselines (EGNN, TFN) while using a fraction of the parameters (e.g., ~59K vs ~29.6M for TFN), which supports the paper's efficiency claim, and the explicit rotation test (train on one orientation, test on 90°-rotated data) is a clean, convincing illustration of why equivariance matters.

Good supplementary rigor: visual illustrations of equivariance (Figures 1-2), detailed complexity analysis of constructing P and Q, and thorough documentation of hyperparameters/architecture choices enabling reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is entirely synthetic (points sampled from randomly generated ellipsoids), with no experiments on real molecular, biomolecular, or physical datasets (e.g., QM9, MD17, protein structures) that are the standard benchmarks for equivariant GNNs and would be necessary to establish practical significance beyond a proof-of-concept.

Only d=3 is tested despite the paper emphasizing the method generalizes to arbitrary d; no ablations on larger/more complex graphs, varying k-NN or ellipsoid parameter regimes, or noise robustness (despite Theorem 3.1 motivating noise robustness, this is never empirically verified).

The datasets are small (512 graphs, 128 nodes each) and the tasks (diameter prediction, synthetic normal-vector field with bandlimited magnitude) are relatively simple/contrived, making it unclear whether the demonstrated performance and parameter efficiency will transfer to tasks with more complex geometric/chemical signal structure where TFN-style high-order equivariant features may matter more.

On the node-level task, TFN still outperforms ESc-GNN (Table 2), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss when/why the proposed method might underperform despite its efficiency, nor explore the apparent tradeoff between expressiveness and parameter count in more depth.

The architecture used in experiments (Section 4, Appendix D) deviates nontrivially from the theoretically analyzed construction in Section 3 (e.g., non-dyadic InfoGain-selected scales, no nonlinearity in scattering coefficients, use of Dirac features, gated sums, invariant feature extraction), and while the authors assert theoretical guarantees carry over, this is not formally verified, creating a gap between theory and what is actually tested.

Only a single random seed/fold structure (5-fold CV) with no independent runs across different random initializations or dataset generation seeds is reported, and no statistical significance testing is performed despite relatively large standard deviations in several baseline results.

Limited comparison breadth: translation equivariance is not discussed/proven (only SO(d) rotation equivariance is addressed, despite the abstract claiming SE(3)-equivariance), which is a potentially significant mismatch between the claimed scope and the proven theoretical results.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated novel construction (vector diffusion wavelets) that extends scalar diffusion wavelets to vector/tangent-bundle valued signals, grounded in the established vector diffusion maps framework of Singer & Wu.

Provides rigorous theoretical results: frame bounds for the new wavelets (Thm 3.1) and rotational equivariance of both wavelets and scattering coefficients (Thms 3.2, 3.3), with complete proofs in the appendix, including careful handling of the SVD sign ambiguity needed to make the local frames well-defined.

The method is computationally efficient by construction (sparse matrix powers rather than explicit eigendecomposition of the connection Laplacian), and the paper includes a careful complexity analysis (Appendix D).

Experiments span three qualitatively different settings (synthetic ellipsoids, real wind-field reconstruction, neural population recordings), with both node- and graph-level, scalar and vector targets, giving decent breadth.

VDW-GNN is consistently competitive with or better than much larger equivariant baselines (EGNN, TFN) while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and clearly demonstrates the practical importance of equivariance via the non-equivariant ablation and rotated-test-set experiments.
Detailed reproducibility documentation (architecture, hyperparameters, cross-validation, runtimes) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Experimental scale is fairly small (2000 subsampled wind measurements, 128-point ellipsoids, single-day wind snapshot), which limits confidence in generalization to larger/more complex real-world settings.

The neural-recording result (VDW-GNN 0.66 vs MARBLE 0.65) is reported as a win but the paper itself notes the difference is not statistically significant (Wilcoxon test), so the headline claim of outperforming MARBLE is overstated relative to the actual evidence.

The theoretical equivariance/well-definedness relies on assuming singular values of the local PCA frame have no repeated multiplicity; this is a nontrivial assumption that can fail for symmetric or near-symmetric local neighborhoods, and the paper does not empirically probe robustness/failure modes in such degenerate or noisy regimes.

Several practical architecture choices (non-dyadic InfoGain-selected scales, added Dirac scalar features, sigmoid gating) deviate from the clean theoretical formulation without much ablation isolating their individual contribution, making it harder to attribute empirical gains specifically to the core VDW construction versus these engineering additions.

The DD-TNN baseline (most directly comparable prior tangent-bundle method) underperforms dramatically (12.76 vs 2.75 MSE) with limited discussion of why, raising questions about whether the baseline was tuned fairly.

No evaluation on standard, widely-used equivariant-GNN benchmarks (e.g., N-body simulation, molecular property prediction) that would allow easier comparison to the broader equivariant GNN literature and more confidently establish generality/significance of the contribution.

The per-node local SVD cost scales cubically in ambient dimension D and with neighborhood size, which could become a bottleneck for higher-dimensional or denser graphs; this scalability limit is acknowledged but not empirically stress-tested.

strengths: The paper presents a clean theoretical extension of diffusion wavelets to vector-valued signals via a vector diffusion matrix Q built from local PCA frames (following Singer & Wu's vector diffusion maps), and proves frame bounds (Thm 3.1) and rotational equivariance of the wavelets and scattering coefficients (Thms 3.2, 3.3), with full proofs provided in the appendix.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad, spanning synthetic point clouds (node- and graph-level), a real wind-field reconstruction task, and an inductive neural-population representation-learning task, with multiple relevant baselines (LEGS, GCN/GAT/GIN, EGNN, TFN, DD-TNN, MARBLE, CEBRA, LFADS).

The method is shown to be far more parameter-efficient than equivariant alternatives (EGNN, TFN) while remaining competitive, and the complexity analysis (Appendix D) together with reported per-epoch timings gives some insight into computational cost.

The authors are honest about some negative/neutral results, e.g., reporting that the improvement over MARBLE on the neural data task is not statistically significant under a paired Wilcoxon test, rather than overselling this result.

The equivariance claims are illustrated with clear visualizations (Figures 3 and 4), and the sign-ambiguity issue in the local SVD construction is explicitly addressed with a concrete fix (Appendix C).
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is fairly incremental: most proofs (Thm 3.1, Lemma A.1) reduce to the scalar diffusion-wavelet frame result via a block/Kronecker-product argument, and the local-frame/Oi,j construction is taken essentially unchanged from Singer & Wu (2012) and closely mirrors the sheaf-Laplacian construction already used by DD-TNN (Battiloro et al., 2024); the main new idea is simply applying a dyadic wavelet filter bank to Q rather than using its heat semigroup directly.

The claim that powers of Q serve as a 'proxy' for the connection-Laplacian heat semigroup e^{-tΔ} is asserted by analogy to the scalar case but is not backed by any approximation/consistency analysis (unlike related manifold-learning works cited by the authors, e.g., Chew et al. 2023), leaving the central modeling assumption theoretically unsupported.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent across tasks: VDW-GNN is second-best (to TFN) on the node-level ellipsoid task, second-best on rotated wind MSE (to EGNN), and on the neural data task its improvement over MARBLE is explicitly not statistically significant — undermining the paper's core significance claim in its most novel, real-world application.

The DD-TNN baseline — designed by its original authors specifically for this exact wind-reconstruction task — underperforms by a very large margin (MSE 12.76 vs. 2.75), which raises concerns about whether the baseline was adequately tuned/reimplemented, and weakens confidence in the comparison.

Experiments are conducted at fairly small scale (n=128 point clouds, 2000 subsampled wind measurements, 44-day neural dataset with per-day models), so the scalability claims in the complexity appendix are not empirically stress-tested on larger, more realistic graphs.

The theoretical setup assumes singular values of local PCA frames have no multiplicity greater than one (needed for SVD uniqueness up to sign), which can be violated for symmetric/isotropic local neighborhoods (e.g., near poles of a sphere or isotropic patches), and the practical robustness of the heuristic sign-flipping fix is not empirically validated.

Translation invariance, highlighted in the abstract as a key symmetry property, is only asserted in a one-line remark rather than proven as a formal theorem, in contrast to the detailed treatment given to rotational equivariance.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel theoretical construct (vector diffusion wavelets, built on vector diffusion maps and the connection Laplacian) that fills a clear gap between scalar diffusion-wavelet GNNs and existing equivariant GNNs designed for vector-valued/tangent-bundle data.

Solid theoretical contributions with complete proofs: frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) analogous to classical diffusion wavelets, and rotational equivariance of both the wavelets (Thm 3.2) and the associated scattering coefficients (Thm 3.3), plus an efficient sparse construction of Q that avoids explicit eigendecomposition (discussed with complexity analysis in Appendix D).

Comprehensive and varied empirical evaluation spanning synthetic point clouds (graph- and node-level, scalar and vector targets), real-world wind-field reconstruction, and real neural population recordings, covering classification, regression, and representation learning tasks.

Strong parameter efficiency: VDW-GNN is competitive with or better than EGNN/TFN while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters (e.g., 59,779 vs 29.6M for TFN in the diameter task), and is also computationally efficient per epoch.

Good choice of strong, relevant baselines (EGNN, TFN, LEGS, GCN/GAT/GIN, plus domain-specific baselines DD-TNN, MARBLE, CEBRA, LFADS), and a more rigorous inductive evaluation protocol for the neural data task than prior work (MARBLE), which is a methodological improvement in its own right.
Scientific honesty: the authors explicitly report that improvement over MARBLE is not statistically significant under a Wilcoxon test rather than overstating the result.
Extensive appendix detailing architecture, hyperparameters, and training protocols supports reproducibility of the reported numbers.
weaknesses: The code availability sentence in the main text is blank/missing a URL ("Our code is available at ."), undermining reproducibility claims despite detailed written descriptions.

Translation invariance, mentioned as a key symmetry in the abstract/intro, is only asserted in a single sentence without a formal theorem or proof, unlike the rotational equivariance results which are rigorously proven.

Margins of improvement in the wind-field experiment are fairly small relative to simpler baselines (e.g., 2.75 vs 2.87 MSE for GCN), and the neural-activity result is statistically indistinguishable from MARBLE, somewhat limiting the strength of the empirical significance claims.

Real-world evaluation is limited to two specialized domains (a single day of wind measurements, one neural dataset); there is no evaluation on more standard/larger geometric deep learning benchmarks (e.g., molecular property prediction, point-cloud segmentation) that would better establish general applicability.

The experiments deviate from the theoretically analyzed dyadic wavelet construction by using non-dyadic, InfoGain-selected scales, introducing additional hyperparameters/complexity not directly covered by the paper's theoretical guarantees (though the authors note the extension is straightforward).

The frame bound in Theorem 3.1 scales with dmax/dmin, which could be loose on graphs with heterogeneous degree distributions; no empirical analysis of how tight/meaningful this bound is in practice is provided.
Synthetic point-cloud experiments are based on relatively simple ellipsoid manifolds, which may not stress-test the method on more topologically complex or noisy manifold settings.
